claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a naturally developed hierarchical heterostructure.
A reduced-order, machine-learning-assisted framework integrating hierarchical heterostructure information will predict Young's modulus faster than full-scale finite element simulations.
The proposed framework will predict yield strength faster than full-scale finite element simulations.
The proposed framework will predict fracture behavior faster than full-scale finite element simulations.
The proposed framework will predict Young's modulus more accurately than full-scale finite element simulations.
The proposed framework will predict yield strength more accurately than full-scale finite element simulations.
The proposed framework will predict fracture behavior more accurately than full-scale finite element simulations.
Grain-boundary distributions, precipitate dispersions, and multiscale heterogeneities will be represented explicitly in the rapid simulation framework.
The hierarchical microstructural features modulate stress distribution.
The hierarchical microstructural features modulate crack-propagation paths.
Representing hierarchical features improves the mapping between microstructural parameters and macroscopic mechanical responses.
The improved microstructure-to-response mapping reduces the simulation complexity required.
Reduced simulation complexity can maintain or enhance predictive accuracy.
The proposed approach will reduce computational time by approximately 10–15% relative to the baseline simulation.
The proposed approach will lower prediction errors relative to experimental measurements compared with established simulation models.
The approach may fail if the framework cannot adequately resolve key hierarchical features.
At high strain rates or varying temperatures, hierarchical microstructural details may lose predictive relevance.
Predictive improvements depend on microstructural-data resolution and the rapid simulation algorithm used.
An error reduction greater than 5% is the declared minimum accuracy improvement.
Failure to achieve both a statistically significant error reduction greater than 5% and an approximately 10–15% runtime reduction is declared to falsify the hypothesis.
